subject: CS
question: How does the syllabus define a Society?

options.text: A physical body of persons united to one another by blood and descent
options.rationale: The syllabus insists that Society is not a physical thing; only the members and their action are physical.

options.text: A group of people living under a written constitution and a settled government
options.rationale: Politics and law are named as institutions that connect a society, but the definition given turns on moral bonds, authority and a common good.

options.text: An enduring union of a number of persons morally bound under authority to cooperate for a common good
A gathering of individuals in one place who happen to share the same interests
options.rationale: The syllabus expressly distinguishes a Society from a crowd; it is the moral bond that makes the difference.

explanation: The syllabus gathers the essential characteristics of a society into a single definition: an enduring union of persons, morally bound under authority, cooperating for a common good.

manualReference.excerpt: Hence, Society may be defined as an enduring union of a number of persons morally bound under authority to cooperate for a common good.
manualReference.citation: Church and Society — THE CHURCH AND THE SOCIETY — Essential Characteristics of a Society (syllabus ¶4730)

subject: CS
question: Outline the essential characteristics of a Society, and state the definition of Society which follows from them.
idealAnswer: The syllabus sets out five essential characteristics of a Society. First, there can be no existing Society without members, and only rational and free beings can form a Society, since it is a union based on agreement about goals. Secondly, the members must be united in a stable or enduring way; a passing association is not a Society. Thirdly, the members must cooperate or work together for the attainment of some end, and this end will be some common good that all the members will share in and that no member could accomplish singly. Fourthly, Society is held together by bonds, and these are moral bonds of means and ends: either the members bind themselves by contract, pledge or agreement, or the bonds are imposed upon them by some law, natural or positive. It is this moral bond that distinguishes a Society from a crowd, that makes the individuals committed members, and that obliges them to their commitment. Fifthly, to guide the cooperative effort to the common good, Society must be equipped with that moral power called authority, authority being the right to determine the means and to direct the members in their use. From these characteristics the syllabus draws its definition: Society may be defined as an enduring union of a number of persons morally bound under authority to cooperate for a common good. The syllabus adds a caution about the nature of a Society: it is not a physical thing. The only thing physical about a Society is the members and their action; the union itself is moral rather than material.

The union is based on agreement about goals
The members must be united in a stable or enduring way
The members must cooperate for the attainment of some end
That end is a common good all share in and none could accomplish singly
Society is held together by moral bonds of means and ends, by contract, pledge or agreement, or imposed by law
The moral bond distinguishes a Society from a crowd
Authority is the moral power that guides the cooperative effort; it is the right to determine the means and direct the members
Definition: an enduring union of a number of persons morally bound under authority to cooperate for a common good
Society is not a physical thing; only the members and their action are physical

subject: CS
question: Discuss the key functions of the Church, with particular reference to its responsibility in and to the society in which it lives.
idealAnswer: The syllabus begins by insisting that the Church is not an institution but a people: the Bible calls it Laos theou, the people of God, a people whose institutions should help them to participate in God's action in the world, that is, in the liberation of man to freedom and responsibility. Its business is the business of Christ, which he himself spelt out in Luke 4:18, 19: to proclaim release to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord. The Church must be, as Harvey Cox puts it, like a confirmed gambler. The Church is in the Society though it is not of it. It is therefore to address the issues that bear on the current political world, current economic problems, high infant mortality rate and the abuse of fundamental human rights. Other areas named are hunger, intra and intertribal conflicts, inadequate housing and poverty; the contamination of water bodies, pollution of the atmosphere and the fast depletion of the natural forest; and human rights abuses and corruption in both government and society, where the Church is to be the voice of the voiceless. Christians are themselves part of the secular society: we live in it, depend on it, and it is in a real sense part of us. No one can function as a Christian, any more than as a human being, independently of the society which has moulded him. The Gospel says that God so loved the world, not only good and religiously minded people, so where men and women are, there the Church must be. There is a great deal of wickedness in the world, but secular does not in itself mean wicked; God does not stop his work when humans stop watching it. All who honestly work for the welfare of human society, whether or not they call themselves believers, may be said to be serving God, for he that is not against us is for us. Finally the Church is to remind Society of two things: that people already have a real experience of God through the secular gifts they take for granted, and that they are in the gravest danger of destroying themselves and their world together if they ignore or defy the law of God and God's transforming grace through the gift of Jesus Christ.

subject: CS
topic: Developments in Modern Understanding of Human Rights
question: Give an account of the significant historical developments in the modern understanding of human rights, from the Magna Carta to the International Bill of Human Rights.
idealAnswer: The syllabus observes that human beings have thought about their duties and rights from the time they decided to live in societies: Plato and Aristotle wrestled with freedom and justice, and Thomas Aquinas and other medieval theologians discussed them in their writings. The modern developments begin in Britain with the Magna Carta, which King John was induced to sign in 1215, and among whose provisions were guarantees of freedom for the Church and of fair trial by one's peers. A second British milestone was the Bill of Rights of 1688-1689, which made the Crown subject to Parliament. The American Declaration of Independence of 1776, drafted by Thomas Jefferson, affirmed as self-evident that all men are created equal and that they are endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights, especially the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Similar language was used in France's Declaration of the Rights of Man and of Citizens, promulgated by its National Assembly in 1789, which speaks of man's natural and inalienable rights. In 1941 President Roosevelt gave his famous State of the Union address, looking forward to a world founded upon essential freedoms: the freedom of every person to worship God in his own way, freedom from want and freedom from fear, adding to each the words everywhere in the world. The United Nations Organization was established in 1945, its charter reaffirming faith in fundamental human rights and in the dignity and worth of the human person, and Article 55 committing it to promote universal respect for human rights without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion. The United Nations then established the Human Rights Commission under the chairmanship of Eleanor, the widow of President Roosevelt, which prepared the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; its first part covers political and civil rights and its second economic, social and cultural rights, and it was adopted by the UN General Assembly in Paris on 10th December 1948, though not all nations ratified it. In 1966 the two International Covenants were published, in 1973 the Helsinki Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe was held, whose Final Act of 1975 included a section on the respect of human rights and fundamental freedoms, and in 1976 the two International Covenants came into effect, so that the long dreamed-of International Bill of Human Rights became a reality.

subject: CS
topic: The Biblical Basis of Human Rights
question: Explain, following John Stott, the biblical basis of human rights under the three words "dignity", "equality" and "responsibility".
idealAnswer: John Stott begins from the questions how human beings have any rights at all, whence they acquired them, and what Christians have distinctively to contribute. His answer is that the origin of human rights is creation: man has never acquired them, nor has any government or other authority conferred them; we received them with our life from our Maker, and they are inherent in our creation. Fundamental to human rights, therefore, is the question of what it means to be human. The biblical basis hinges on three words. Human dignity is based on Genesis 1:27-28, where three issues stand out: our relationship to God, since God created man in his own image, so that we are God-like beings whose rational, moral and spiritual qualities separate us from the animals and relate us to God; our relationship to one another, since male and female he created them, from which it follows that sexuality is God's creation, marriage his institution and human companionship his purpose, so that whoever abuses these abuses God; and our relationship to the earth and its creatures, since God gave us dominion with instructions to subdue and cultivate the earth, from which are derived the right to work and to rest, to share in the earth's resources, to food, clothing and shelter, and to life and health. Christians may also speak of a surpassing dignity derived from the Creator redeeming and recreating us through the incarnation and atonement of his Son. Human equality follows: the tragedy, Stott says, is that human rights have not always meant equal rights, because the good gifts of the Creator are spoiled by human selfishness, so that the rights God gave to all equally degenerate into my rights on which I insist. The God we worship shows no partiality, and Moses told Israel that the Lord is the God who shows no partiality and accepts no bribes, so Israelite judges were to do justice to the small and the great alike (Deuteronomy 10:17-18). All human rights violations contradict the equality we enjoy by creation, and he who oppresses the poor shows contempt for their Maker (Proverbs 14:31). Human responsibility is the last word derived from our createdness: whenever rights are emphasised to the exclusion of responsibility we miss the biblical pattern, for the Bible calls us to defend other people's rights but, when it addresses us, emphasises our responsibilities. Our responsibility is to secure the other person's rights, forgoing our own in order to do so. Jesus Christ is the supreme model of this renunciation (Philippians 2:6-7), and Paul, who had rights as an apostle, renounced them for the sake of the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9).
keyPoints: The origin of human rights is creation; they were neither acquired nor conferred
Dignity rests on Genesis 1:27-28 and three relationships
Relationship to God: made in his image, with rational, moral and spiritual qualities
Relationship to one another: male and female; sexuality, marriage and companionship are God's
Relationship to the earth: dominion grounds the material and economic rights
A surpassing dignity from redemption through the incarnation and atonement
Equality: God shows no partiality; violations contradict the equality of creation
Responsibility: the Bible emphasises our duties, not our rights
Christ (Philippians 2:6-7) and Paul (1 Corinthians 9) as models of renouncing rights

subject: CS
question: Discuss the inherent weaknesses of democracy identified in the syllabus, and show how the Church can help to sustain democracy.
idealAnswer: Churchill remarked that democracy is the worst form of government except for all the others: it is not perfect, but it is better than any other form known to man. The syllabus identifies seven inherent weaknesses and attaches to each a suggestion for the Church. The Tyranny of Democracy is the tendency of politicians to look out for the interest of the majority while neglecting or abusing the rights of the minority, which is especially dangerous where the majority is of a particular racial, ethnic, religious or ideological orientation; the Church can help ensure that government is fair to all its constituents and that minority rights are protected. The Fallacy of Democracy is committed when one defends the tyranny of the majority by arguing that democracy is by definition the rule of the majority; this is a conceptual blunder, since majority rule does not imply minority suffering, and the Church can expose the error and press for non-discrimination, a role supported by Galatians 3:28. The Disease of Democracy is the frequent election of representatives who make wonderful promises, fail to keep them, and attend to their constituents only when re-election is near; the Church should educate members to study candidates carefully and should train and encourage altruistic mature Christians to stand for office. Red Tapeism is the tendency to complicate and unduly delay administrative and legal procedures, breeding frustration, bribery and even resort to arms; the Church should advise those in administration to minimise delays, and should organise experienced church leaders, superannuated clergy, lawyers and retired judges and magistrates into Christian Family Arbitration Centres to settle cases out of court and decongest the legal system. Democracy is also a Catalyst for Ethnic Conflicts, since previously oppressed groups seize the opportunity of the prevailing wind of change, and the right to self determination in particular, to separate from their former oppressors; churches in conflict-prone areas must be part of the early warning system, keep security agents informed, and preach and counsel against such destabilising moves. The Problem of Vagueness arises because the tenets of democracy - freedom, justice, equality, peace, unity - are inherently vague and ambiguous, so that it is difficult to determine when they have been achieved; the Church can sensitise people to this ambiguity and to how such terms are manipulated by political adventurers and opposition parties. Finally there is Vulnerability to Military Coups: Africa alone has witnessed about fifty coups, in all of which corruption is cited as a common major cause; through military chaplains, guest preachers to the barracks and the mass media the Church should show that corruption is part of human nature and cannot be removed by coups, and should commend the checks and balances of democracy and the removal of corrupt politicians through the ballot box without bloodshed. In addition, the churches should pray for the state and supplement government's efforts by establishing schools, vocational and technical institutes and agricultural research centres.

question: Explain why, according to Kantiok, African Christians should participate in politics.
idealAnswer: The syllabus takes this material from an article in the ABC Commentary. Kantiok argues that the unwillingness of many Christians to take part in politics is partly rooted in a failure to distinguish between party politics and political participation. Political participation, he says, includes exercising one's right to vote and be voted for, speaking out against any wrongdoing by those in power, and holding leaders accountable for their actions. He observes that while Christians tend to avoid political participation, Muslims understand its importance, and consequently control political power in many African states, even where they are a minority; unlike Christians they do not believe in the separation of church and state, because that encourages secularism. Kantiok adds that Jesus too did not separate religion and politics: in his mission statement in Luke 4:18-19 he declared that his ministry was to those suffering various forms of bondage and oppression, including economic oppression, that is poverty, physical oppression, that is disease and disabilities, political oppression, that is injustice and oppressive rule, and demonic oppression, that is various forms of occult practices. Other biblical examples of political participation include Joseph in Egypt, who saved many from hunger and starvation (Genesis 41), Amos, who warned the political leaders of his time against injustice, Daniel and his three friends, and Nehemiah. In the New Testament Paul refused to give up his rights as a citizen when the political authorities put him in prison and flogged him without giving him a proper trial (Acts 16:37-38; 22:25). Kantiok therefore advises that moral bankruptcy, corruption, poverty, disease and ignorance all clearly call for Christian participation in politics, and concludes that African Christians need to understand that the destinies of their nations rest on their political participation.

subject: CS
question: What are the six common sources of conflict identified in the syllabus? Explain each briefly.
idealAnswer: The syllabus identifies six common causes of conflict. The first is differences in perception: no two individuals perceive things in the same way, and this often leads to misunderstanding, confusion and conflict. The second is differences in priority or values. Values are deeply held beliefs, and conflicts often develop when people with different value systems try to work together; value conflicts arise over differences in religious, moral, ideological or philosophical outlooks, and where conflict concerns values people have difficulty in changing their stand. The third is differences in expectations or role pressures: conflicts often arise over different expectations when these are not fulfilled, as when one person says I wanted you to and the other replies I expected you to. The fourth is divergent goals. The syllabus illustrates this with Yaw Nkrumah and Kwadwo Nsiah, who work for the same organisation but in different departments: Yaw wants to help the company make more profit by improving the quality of their products while Kwadwo wants more profit by decreasing costs; this leads to competition among managers for available resources, and lack of team effort can develop into enormous conflict situations. The fifth is self-esteem or status threat: Yaw may have a good idea, but Kwadwo's self-esteem depends on his having all the good ideas, and since Kwadwo is the boss and bosses know best, status and authority become sources of anger and frustration. The sixth is personality clashes: troublesome individuals have hostile natures and are predisposed toward conflict, people with strong needs to bully use their jobs to express hostility, and individuals with low self-esteem often overcompensate by being belligerent or hostile toward other people.

subject: CS
question: Outline the five principles which Tokunboh Adeyemo proposes for resolving conflicts, together with the biblical examples he cites.
idealAnswer: Tokunboh Adeyemo, in his article in the ABC Commentary, writes that when we manage a conflict we simply organise, regulate and take charge of it in order to make it serve a good cause. He says that in resolving any conflict there are three key questions to ask: what are we agreeing or disagreeing about, why are we agreeing or disagreeing, and how can we get past this and move forward. He then proposes five principles. The first is honest communication: silence and isolation deepen misunderstanding, which fuels conflict; in Genesis 13:1-18 Abraham did not gloss over the potential for quarrels between his herdsmen and those of Lot, but discussed it openly with Lot and developed an appropriate strategy to deal with it. The second is getting beneath surface issues and unseen motives: often the apparent cause of a conflict is not the real issue, the conflict being rooted in people's underlying motives and beliefs which they may not have clearly identified; in Genesis 26:19-31 the real problem between the people of Gerar and Isaac went beyond water. The third is negotiation: the best way to find peace is through a process of give and take in which neither party insists on being the winner, and the story of 1 Kings 12 shows the disastrous consequence of Rehoboam's unwillingness to negotiate. The fourth is external intervention: the parties may be so caught up in the conflict that they have difficulty talking to one another and reaching agreement, in which case the assistance of a neutral person such as a marriage counsellor, or of an organisation such as the United Nations, may be sought; in Acts 15:1-2 Paul and Barnabas and their opponents took their case to the apostles in Jerusalem. The fifth is divine intervention: there is a spiritual dimension to conflicts, so in resolving them we need to seek divine assistance, and the Council at Jerusalem resolved the crisis that would have permanently divided the church into Jews and Gentiles (Acts 15:23-29).

chapter: RELIGIOUS PLURALISM AND THE CHRISTIAN MESSAGE
question: Explain why B. J. Van der Walt describes secularism as the most dangerous enemy of Christianity.
idealAnswer: Van der Walt concludes his discussion by describing secularism as the most dangerous enemy of Christianity, and draws attention to the conclusion of the World Mission Conference held in Jerusalem in 1982, that no student of the deeper problems of life can fail to see that the greatest rival of Christianity in the world today is not Mohammedanism, or Buddhism, or Hinduism, or Confucianism, but a worldwide secular way of life and interpretation of the nature of things. He gives three reasons in support. First, secularism is not an open enemy attacking the Christian faith with physical weaponry; it works practically unnoticed, and in a subtle way it infiltrates and undermines faith. Secondly, it works gradually from the outside to the inside: from the outside it might seem as if the Christian faith is still in order while living communion with God has in reality ceased to exist, and the process is so gradual that mostly we do not notice it any more, so that when we ultimately realise that an institution or the whole of life has been secularised it is already too late. Thirdly, it is not a clearly discernible and definable phenomenon: it is a sort of chameleon ideology, the medium for the growth of a variety of ideologies which in turn further promote the process of secularisation. Van der Walt nevertheless believes that we should neither under-estimate nor over-estimate the power of secularism, because the Gospel of Jesus Christ has power to conquer it. He concludes that only a radical, total, integral Christian worldview will be able to break the formidable power of secularism, not only in theory but concretely: in family life, in education, in politics, in the world of commerce and labour and even in the church. The syllabus adds that the Bible's clear response to this way of life is found in the Book of Ecclesiastes, where Solomon on reflection of his life found that it is a chasing after the wind, and that Yusufu Turaki advises that religion provides ethical and social values which affect people in their private and public lives and makes for responsible living, so that Christians must exhibit their Christian life (Matthew 5:13-16) in our secularised and materialistic societies in order to have influence.

topic: The Position of the Methodist Church Ghana
question: State and explain the position of the Methodist Church Ghana on divorce, dissolution of marriage and remarriage as set out in Standing Order 743.
idealAnswer: The position of the Methodist Church Ghana is found in Standing Order 743 of the Constitution, under the title Divorce, Dissolution of Marriage and Remarriage, as quoted from the Constitution and Standing Orders of the Methodist Church Ghana, 2000 Revised Edition. Its first provision is that no Member of the Church shall dissolve his or her marriage without first consulting his or her Minister, who shall make every effort to reconcile the parties and shall, if need be, seek the assistance of the Leader's Meeting. Secondly, if one partner fails in fulfilling the obligations of marriage, it is the duty of the other, as a Christian, to be active in seeking reconciliation so long as any possibility of it remains. Thirdly, where all efforts to effect reconciliation fail, the Leader's Meeting shall be informed of this. Fourthly, when one party has already formed a union with a third person and is judged to be beyond hope of restoration to the lawful partner, the latter may be permitted to dissolve the marriage by the appropriate process under the ordinance or Customary Law, and shall then be free to re-marry in due course; but this permission to divorce and re-marry is subject to confirmation by the Bishop of the Diocese, who shall act in consultation with the Circuit Superintendent concerned and a small committee, including a lawyer, appointed by Synod. Finally, any Member who dissolves his or her marriage against the advice of the Minister and the Leader's Meeting, or who is the guilty party in divorce proceedings, or who contravenes S.O. 742 (3) (1), shall be subject to the discipline of the Leader's Meeting. The syllabus adds that the peace or freedom principle established by Paul as a basis for divorce in mixed-faith marriages, resting on 1 Corinthians 7:15, may be extended to other cases after all efforts have been made to save a marriage, and that this appears to be the spirit of S.O. 743.

subject: CS
question: Describe the effects of divorce, and explain how the church should assist those who are going through it.
idealAnswer: The syllabus says that for most people divorce brings pain and turmoil, and affects people in many ways. There are emotional effects, including anxiety, guilt, fear, sadness, depression, anger, bitterness and frustration. There are behavioural effects, including declining work productivity and difficulties in completing routine tasks. There are social effects, including changing relationships with family, friends, work colleagues and fellow church members. There are physical effects, including increased illness and declining health. There are spiritual effects, in which some people draw closer to Christ while others drift away. And there are harmful effects on the children, even when the divorcing couple tries to make the separation smooth for them, and even upon adult offspring. The effects of divorce on the couple have been compared to what happens when one attempts to separate two sheets of paper which have been glued together: however carefully and skilfully this is done, the two sheets never get separated without each sheet being torn and damaged at several points. That, the syllabus says, is why Christians and the church must give prayerful support to those going through divorce and to the already divorced, as well as to the children and others who may be caught up in the tension. While the church must seek all available means to help couples to be faithful to the end, the rules against divorce cannot be handled mechanically. They must be applied with concern, understanding and prayer support, and in ways that will lighten the hurt, disappointment and burden of persons finding themselves in this situation.

subject: CS
question: Describe five challenges that a marriage may face, and suggest how each may be met.
idealAnswer: The syllabus lists a number of challenges which, if not well handled, can lead to divorce, noting that the list is not exhaustive and that every couple must identify their own. The first is financial strain. One does not have to be rich to have a successful marriage, but lack of money for the basic needs of the family puts a strain on the relationship, and some couples plunge into this just after the wedding through failure to do proper financial planning on a short and long term basis. It can only be overcome by combining proper planning, hard work and a lifestyle which suits one's pocket instead of following what others do, and by being faithful to God, trusting him to give us the ability to create wealth (Deuteronomy 8:18); 1 Timothy 5:8 warns that whoever does not provide for his own household has denied the faith. The second is childlessness, a big challenge in cultures where childbearing is regarded as the principal reason for marriage; the woman is often falsely accused of barrenness, and the results include depression, disappointment, anxiety, shock, anger and feelings of sexual inadequacy. Since the causes may include infertility, miscarriage or loss of a child shortly after birth, the couple should seek medical guidance and appropriate marriage counsellors, show solidarity with each other, remember their vows, and after seeking medical help trust God and leave everything to his sovereign will; the godly offspring God desires (Malachi 2:15) does not involve biological children alone. The third is sexual unfulfilment, which arises where one partner feels not sufficiently catered for sexually, whether through differing levels of desire, misinformation about sex, harmful cultural values, the impact of pornography, busy lifestyles, stress and boredom, illness, psychological blocks or sexual dysfunction; it lowers self-esteem and may lead to involvement with alternative sexual activities and eventually to separation or divorce, so couples need to seek solutions to the basic causes with competent professionals. The fourth is the failure to keep the romance alive, which the syllabus compares to failing to nourish a child after birth, leading automatically to Kwashiorkor; the key is to continue with those practices that attracted one to the other during the pre-marital relationship, to make time for each other, and to take up hobbies and pastimes they enjoy, God himself having inspired the most romantic book in the world, the Song of Solomon. A fifth is my children versus my spouse, where more attention is given to the children at the expense of the spouse and parents take sides with the children, as happened with Isaac and Rebecca over Jacob and Esau; the couple must remember that the union before the altar was between husband and wife, and that the children will in future be united to their own partners. Other challenges named include transparency in times of prosperity, my spouse versus my career, travel abroad and the long absence of one partner, illustrated by Elimelech's family and Naomi returning alone as Marah, the little foxes of Song of Songs 2:15, and demonic influences, against which the couple's greatest weapon is the sharing of their spiritual lives, studying God's word and praying together.

subject: CS
chapter: SEXUAL PERVERSION - WHAT IS THE BIBLICAL VIEW?
topic: What the Church Fathers and Reformers Say
question: Give an account of what the church fathers, the medieval church and the Reformers are reported in the syllabus as saying about homosexual practice.
idealAnswer: The syllabus reports that the early church condemned the homosexual life-style as contrary to the spirit of the Gospel, and that such practices were denounced mainly on the grounds that they are in themselves unnatural. Tertullian wrote that all other frenzies of the lusts which exceed the laws of nature are impious towards both human bodies and sexes, and that they are banished not only from the threshold but also from all shelter of the Church, for they are not sins so much as monstrosities. John Chrysostom denounced such practices as unnatural, and in his commentary on Romans 1:26-27 observed that the delights of sodomy are an unpardonable insult to nature; he held such immoralities to be doubly destructive, first in that they jeopardise the race by deflecting the sexual organs from their primary procreative purpose, and secondly in that they sow disharmony and strife between man and woman, who are no longer impelled by their physical desires to live together peaceably. With reference to Genesis 19, St Augustine wrote that those shameful acts against nature, such as were committed in Sodom, ought everywhere and always to be detested and punished, and that if all nations were to do such things they would equally be held guilty of the same crime by the law of God, which has not so made men that they should use another in this way. The medieval church, the syllabus reports, was pastorally sensitive to the problems of those involved in such practices, but remained uncompromisingly opposed to the practices themselves; since such acts could not lead to procreation, they moved beyond the limits for sexual behaviour, and Thomas Aquinas considered them sins against nature, the most serious genus of sins of lust, no less grievous than bestiality. The major Reformers maintained the same resistance as the early Christians: Luther considered the presence and toleration of homosexual activity among the clergy as one of the worst symptoms of decay in the church, and a product of human failure to know and honour the true God. The syllabus places this material alongside the argument from nature and creation, in which theologians from Thomas Aquinas to Karl Barth relate their understanding of nature to the doctrine of creation, Barth pointing to the way male and female complement each other as people created in the image and likeness of God, and Aquinas stressing the procreative end of heterosexual intercourse.

subject: CS
topic: The Practice of Homosexuality in Ghana
question: Describe, as the syllabus presents it, the forms in which homosexual practice occurs in Ghana, and outline the call to Christian love that the syllabus makes in response.
idealAnswer: The syllabus states that the practice occurs in Ghana in various forms. Public knowledge of the female form, lesbianism, limited it to the practice of supi in the boarding system of high schools: the system whereby some girls take other girls in the school as sexual partners and engage in sexual activities in tents, that is student beds covered by bed sheets. In most cases the senior girls take advantage of innocent fresh students, and there are stories of junior students bullied into such relationships by seniors. Some lesbian relationships involve female tutors and female students; the syllabus reports a case in a female church institution where a student became involved with a foreign woman on the staff, an affair which lasted a long time and left the Ghanaian lady emotionally devastated and eventually mentally unwell after the foreigner left the country. The male form, sodomy, was until recent times prevalent among prison inmates, and compared with supi among girls the incidence of sodomy in boys' schools has been far less. Thus until recently homosexuality in Ghana was associated with institutional life, in prisons and schools; today it has spread outside the institutions to hotels, guest houses, student hostels and private homes, and although the practice is outlawed, youth and adults of both sexes are involved in it for carnal pleasure and for money, with same sex prostitution and partnerships gaining root underground. A further factor in its growth is sex tourism: some tourists visit the country for sexual adventures, and young people have been lured into same sex prostitution by the attractive cash payments, one reported incident involving local boys, European tourists and photographs intercepted by customs officers at the parcel section of the Post Office. Homosexual marriages remain unknown in Ghana because of the law, though in the name of human rights the international gay movement would join hands with local counterparts to lobby for recognition; South Africa is perhaps the only country in Africa that now permits same sex marriages. The syllabus then insists on a distinction between homosexual inclination or inversion, for which people may not be responsible, and homosexual acts, for which they are. In its call to Christian love it defines homophobia as the negative attitude of personal hatred and fear towards homosexuals, a mixture of irrational fear, hostility and even revulsion, which overlooks the fact that many are probably not responsible for their condition though they are for their conduct. Richard Lovelace calls for a double repentance: that gay people should renounce their homosexual lifestyle, and that the straight ones should renounce homophobia. At the heart of the homosexual condition, the syllabus says, is a deep loneliness, a natural human hunger for mutual love, a search for identity and a longing for completeness, which must be met in the local church family. It adds that the fact that some people are homosexual does not mean that very close same-sex friendships are to be discouraged, and points to Ruth and Naomi, David and Jonathan, and Paul and Timothy as healthy friendships in the Bible, while cautioning that such relationships should not be allowed to degenerate.
